subject: An open-source agent just edged out humans
preheader: Prime Agent beat the human ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, loops replaced prompts, and my own numbers prove the compounding case.

title.lead: The leap didn't come from a new model.
title.muted: It came from the scaffolding around it.

dek: A weekly field note from Art of the Possible.
editorNote: Every story this week is the same story told five ways: the model isn't where the action is any more, the scaffolding around it is. An open-source harness just nudged past the human benchmark on ARC-AGI-3 without any ARC-specific training. A template library turned 'loop engineering' from a viral thread into something you can install. And my own Instagram numbers went from 152 views to 6,593 in three months while my editing skills stayed exactly the same.

If you take one thing from this issue: start using AI somewhere it only gets you halfway today. The harnesses, loops, and context you build around it are what turn 50% into 90% by the next model release.

title.lead: An agent just edged out humans on ARC-AGI-3.
title.muted: The breakthrough is the harness, not the model.

stories.hook: Prime Agent scored 95.5% on the benchmark built to test human-like reasoning; the human baseline is 95.4%.
whatShipped: Prime Intellect released Prime Agent, a self-improving agent harness that can rewrite its own prompts, memories, and skills, and spawn new sub-agents as it works. On the ARC-AGI-3 public demo it reports 95.5%, slightly above the 95.4% human benchmark, running on Opus 5 with no ARC-specific training. For context: when ARC-AGI-3 launched four months ago, frontier models were barely reaching 30%, and the much-loved OpenClaw scores about 5% on the community leaderboard.
stories.whyItMatters: ARC-AGI-1 stood unbeaten for five years. ARC-AGI-2 fell within a year. ARC-AGI-3 fell in four months, and the jump came from the harness layer, not a new model. The scaffolding around a model can now change its performance more than the model itself. ARC Prize notes community ARC-AGI-3 scores are self-reported.

lever.label: Build on the repo
lever.body: The whole harness is open source. Clone it and point the self-improving loop at your own hardest long-running tasks.

takeaways: Current frontier models alone score under 30% on ARC-AGI-3; the harness closed the gap to human level.
Self-rewriting prompts, memories, and skills mean the agent gets smarter as it runs.

media.alt: Rich on camera with the ARC-AGI-3 score chart showing Prime Agent at 95.5% above the 95.4% human baseline

stories.emailSummary: An open-source, self-improving agent harness reports 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3's public demo, a hair above the 95.4% human benchmark, with no ARC-specific training. The leap came from the harness layer, and you can build on the repo today.

title.lead: Stop using AI like a chatbot.
title.muted: Build loops that run your business instead.

stories.hook: Loopany packages 'loop engineering' into templates that act, review their own results, and self-improve.
whatShipped: Loopany, built by Jason Zhou (whose 'loop engineering is the future, not prompt engineering' thread pulled 510K views on X), is a template library of AI loops for growth, operations, coding, and day-to-day grind work. Every loop is four simple parts: a trigger that runs the agent on a schedule, a task file defining what good looks like, a memory file where results and learnings accumulate, and a process that folds that memory back into the task file so the loop genuinely improves each cycle.
stories.whyItMatters: A chatbot forgets you between sessions. A loop compounds: I'm running the SEO loop on my own page, and it finds keywords, drafts the blogs, and monitors results after publishing, getting better at all three as the memory file grows.

lever.label: Install a loop
lever.body: Pick one template that matches a weekly chore, wire the trigger + task file + memory file + update step, and let it run for a month before judging it.

takeaways: Trigger, task file, memory file, self-update: every useful loop is those four things.
The self-update step is the one most people skip, and it is the whole point.

media.alt: Rich beneath an animated four-node cycle diagram: trigger, task file, memory file, self-update

stories.emailSummary: Loopany turns loop engineering into installable templates. Four parts per loop: a scheduled trigger, a task file, a memory file, and a step that folds learnings back in so the loop improves every cycle.

title.muted: My editing skills didn't change. The models did.

stories.hook: Two of my own Reels, side by side, with the real numbers on screen.
whatShipped: I put my first AI-edited Reel from May next to one from last week: 152 views versus 6,593. I edit the same way for both, dumping raw footage in and letting AI produce the video largely independently. The main thing that changed in between was the models. The funny part: that first video was me arguing that compounding is the reason to start using AI early, and it just proved its own thesis.
stories.whyItMatters: If you wait for AI to be perfect at a task before adopting it, you also skip the period where your accumulated feedback and context push a 50% result to 70-80%. Then the next model release lands on top of your scaffolding, not on zero.

lever.label: The instruction
lever.body: Pick something AI can't quite do for you yet and start doing it anyway. You're building the context that future model releases will multiply.

takeaways: Adopt at 50% quality; compound to 90% through feedback plus model releases.
The receipts are real: same editor, same pipeline, 43x the views.

media.alt: Two Instagram Reels side by side labelled 152 views, 3 months ago and 6,593 views, last week

stories.emailSummary: Same editor, same AI-driven pipeline, three months apart: 152 views versus 6,593. The compounding argument from my first video just proved itself on my own account.

title.lead: Good at everything comes down to three things.

stories.hook: One setup pattern that works for work, relationships, learning, and fitness alike.
whatShipped: The whole playbook in one Reel. One: context engineering, a file system per life domain, with instructions for AI to pull relevant context into conversations and update the files as it learns. Two: skills, training the AI to do a task exactly how you would; if you repeat a task more than twice, make it a skill. Three: automations, scheduled tasks in Claude, so routine weekly work kicks off on its own and your life starts running on autopilot.
stories.whyItMatters: This is the personal version of the harness story: the person who wins with AI isn't the one with the best prompts, it's the one whose context, skills, and schedules are already in place when the next model arrives.

lever.label: The rule of thumb
lever.body: Repeating a task more than twice? Turn it into a skill. Doing it weekly? Turn it into a scheduled task.

takeaways: One file system per domain of your life, kept current by the AI itself.
Skills encode how you do things; automations decide when they happen.

media.alt: Rich as a silhouette over an editorial photo collage, with the line: how to become freaking good at everything

stories.emailSummary: Context engineering, skills, and scheduled automations: the three-part setup pattern that makes AI compound in any domain of your life.

title.muted: You've never heard of any of these.

stories.hook: Ten niche AI references, rattled off in one breath, that separate depth from feed-level fluency.
whatShipped: Ten names in fourteen seconds: LangGraph, Gavin Baker, NVIDIA NIMs, fine-tuning, Dwarkesh Patel, harness engineering, JEPA, latent space, model adaptation strategies, and Greenline. Each one gets a card with a one-line 'what it is' as it's spoken. It's a self-test: how many could you explain to a colleague?
stories.whyItMatters: Generic AI content teaches you the same five tools everyone already knows. The compounding advantage lives one layer down, in the harnesses, architectures, and voices that shape what ships six months from now.

lever.label: The self-test
lever.body: Count how many of the ten you could actually explain. Pick the two you couldn't and go one layer deep on each this week.

takeaways: Fluency with the feed is not depth; these ten are a quick depth audit.

media.alt: Rich in a rounded picture-in-picture with rapid-fire cards naming ten niche AI references

stories.emailSummary: Ten niche AI references in one breath, LangGraph to JEPA to Greenline. A fourteen-second depth audit: how many could you explain?

subject: AI left the chat box this week
preheader: A workday that writes itself, an animated site, a tech power map, open voice and the honest outtakes.

title.lead: AI left the chat box this week.
title.muted: Here are five things I made with it.

dek: A weekly field note from Art of the Possible: what shipped, why it matters, and the lever you can copy.
editorNote: AI stopped being a chat window this week. It watched a workday, spoke back in real time, rebuilt a website and rewired an information diet. The common thread is that the model is disappearing into the tool. You notice the result before you notice the AI.

These are the five things I made to understand that shift. I have kept the useful bit from each one: the repo, the template, the workflow, or the honest version of what it took to ship. Start with whichever one solves a problem you actually have.

stories.hook: Dayflow turns everything you did on your Mac into a useful journal, without asking you to log a thing.
whatShipped: Dayflow is an open-source Mac app that watches your screen in the background and writes the journal of your workday. No timers, tags or notes. It reconstructs the day as a clean timeline of what you were actually doing.
You can choose a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, which keeps the analysis on your machine. Cloud providers are optional, not required.
stories.whyItMatters: The interesting part is not another productivity dashboard. Local models can now make sense of sensitive personal context without shipping it to somebody else's server. That unlocks software that works precisely because the AI lives with you.

lever.label: Build on the repo
lever.body: Install the app, run the local-model path, then treat its timeline as a starting point for the workflow you wish your computer understood automatically.

takeaways: Passive products beat habits that depend on remembering.
Local is a capability choice; cloud providers remain optional.

media.alt: Rich presenting a Dayflow Reel with the headline This is the future of AI startups

stories.emailSummary: An open-source Mac app turns your screen activity into a work journal, with a fully local AI option.

title.lead: The shortcut to an animated website.

stories.hook: The best AI websites rarely begin with a blank prompt. They begin with taste, a proven template and a good substitution brief.
whatShipped: I used a three-step workflow to make the animated newsletter page you are looking at: Pinterest for direction, Midjourney and Gemini for the visual assets, then a proven motion prompt from motionsites.ai.
The final step was deliberately simple: paste the template into Claude and tell it exactly which images and video should replace the placeholders.
stories.whyItMatters: AI rewards iteration and art direction more than heroic one-shot prompting. Starting from a strong structure lets you spend your time choosing and refining, rather than persuading a model to rediscover a pattern somebody already solved.

lever.label: The three-step recipe
lever.body: 1. Find the visual direction. 2. Borrow a motion pattern that already works. 3. Ask Claude to swap in your assets without changing the interaction model.

takeaways: Use Midjourney for divergent visual exploration.
Use Gemini for precise edits and video generation.
Use Claude to adapt the implementation, not invent the whole brief.

media.alt: Rich presenting three animated mobile website examples with the headline Level up your website the easy way

stories.emailSummary: A three-step visual, template and substitution workflow for building animated AI websites without starting from scratch.

title.lead: Nine million follows reveal who shapes tech.

stories.hook: Digg used the X social graph to rank the people whose followings carry the strongest signal across AI, startups and investing.
whatShipped: Digg mapped roughly nine million follow relationships to show how the tech community connects. The ranking surfaces people, companies and politicians actively shaping technology, with category views for AI, founders, investors and more.
The useful surface is the ranking itself: a set of names and categories you can use to rebuild a more deliberate information diet.
stories.whyItMatters: The editorial bet is information timing: a feed built around people doing the work should expose you to stronger ideas earlier than a feed optimised for mass reach. Curating your inputs remains one of the highest-leverage ways to improve what you know.

lever.label: Curate the algorithm
lever.body: Pick one field you want to understand, open the matching category, and follow the first ten people whose work is genuinely relevant. Do not copy the whole leaderboard; build a deliberate signal set.

takeaways: Ranked followers are a different signal from raw audience size.
Digg does not publish the exact gravity formula, so treat it as discovery rather than truth.

media.alt: Rich presenting a Reel about the most influential technology people on X

stories.emailSummary: Digg mapped nine million X follows into a practical discovery layer for tech's highest-signal voices.

title.lead: The content engine has a human inside.

stories.hook: Teaching people about AI and startups also means repeatedly forgetting how sentences work in front of a camera.
whatShipped: This 32-second compilation is the honest layer underneath the polished explainers: missed lines, resets and the strange reality of becoming an on-camera creator because you wanted to teach what you were building.
It is lighter than the four builds above, but it belongs in the week because it is what shipping the other four actually looked like.
stories.whyItMatters: A repeatable system should make the work easier without pretending the work is frictionless. Showing the resets is part of building in public, and a useful antidote to the idea that everybody else ships perfectly on the first take.

lever.label: Keep the rough cut
lever.body: Save the resets. The failed takes are useful feedback on the script, and occasionally they are the most human thing you made all week.

takeaways: Friction is evidence, not a personal defect.
A good system preserves the human parts worth sharing.

media.alt: Rich on camera under a caption about realising that teaching AI and startups means making content

stories.emailSummary: The unpolished reality behind the week's four builds: resets, missed lines and one useful reminder to keep the rough cut.

title.lead: Open voice AI already feels live.

stories.hook: A real-time Hugging Face demo can hold a fast conversation, search the web and reason over a screenshot.
whatShipped: I tested an open-source real-time voice workflow rather than another polished assistant demo. In this test it responded quickly, searched the web, read a screenshot and moved between tasks without forcing the conversation back into a text box.
That is enough to imagine the next layer: tutors that can see the work, accessibility tools that can explain a screen, and home assistants that are useful because they understand context.
stories.whyItMatters: The demo suggests voice stops feeling like a novelty when latency gets low enough and the model can use tools. The interaction becomes closer to directing a collaborator than dictating into software.

lever.label: Start from an open demo
lever.body: Use a working real-time voice Space or repository as the harness, then add one narrow tool that makes the conversation useful for a real job.

takeaways: Low latency changes what users are willing to say aloud.
Tool use matters more than a perfect synthetic voice.

media.alt: Rich presenting a Reel with the headline You can now build anything with Voice AI

stories.emailSummary: A hands-on real-time voice demo shows why low latency plus tools turns speech into a serious interface.
